analysis.one_liner: Lets states use Medicaid drug rebates to give residents discounted prescription prices.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee on March 25 and 27, 2009, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill lets a state set up a prescription drug discount program by requiring drug manufacturers to pay the state the same rebates they already pay under Medicaid for drugs sold through the program. At least 95% of those rebates must go to residents earning up to roughly three times the poverty line as lower drug prices, and states are not required to spend their own money. Manufacturers would have to agree as a condition of participating in the Medicaid drug rebate program.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states that opt in, earning up to 300% of the federal poverty line, who would get lower prices at the pharmacy counter without a new taxpayer cost. State governments also gain a tool to cut drug costs for residents using federal rebate money rather than state funds.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Moderate-income residents of states that opt in

how_it_helps.text: Drug manufacturers must pay state discount programs the same rebates they pay under Medicaid, as a condition of participating in the Medicaid outpatient drug rebate agreement.
At least 95% of the rebates a state receives must be passed to eligible residents as discounted prices on outpatient prescription drugs.
Eligible residents are state residents with income up to a percentage of the poverty line set by the state, capped at 300%.
States are not required to spend their own money on the program, may add state funds for larger subsidies, and need no Section 1115 waiver to run it.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and generic drug manufacturers, who would pay rebates on a new pool of drug sales they currently sell at full list price. If they raise prices elsewhere or limit participation to offset it, other purchasers could feel some effect.

drawbacks.text: Coverage is limited to residents with income at or below 300% of the poverty line; people above that line get nothing from the program.

Because the rebates are mandatory for any manufacturer that participates in Medicaid, manufacturers face a take-it-or-leave-it choice between paying new rebates and dropping out of the entire Medicaid drug rebate agreement, a structure that could push prices up elsewhere in the market.
The bill creates no federal program and only takes effect in states that opt in, so its reach depends entirely on state-level choices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to moderate-income residents is direct and concrete: lower out-of-pocket drug costs funded by manufacturer rebates rather than new taxes. The main trade-offs are the income cutoff that leaves out higher earners and the pressure the mandatory-rebate structure puts on manufacturers, which could show up as higher prices outside the program. On balance the bill is a targeted help for people struggling with drug costs, funded by an industry that currently sells to this group at full price.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, sat there without a markup or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Van Hollen introduced the bill on March 25, 2009, with four original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction.
Two days later, on March 27, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
The action history shows no further action for the remainder of the 111th Congress: no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote.
The bill drew 7 cosponsors, all House Democrats, by the end of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers are better off: they kept selling to people at full price without paying state discount-program rebates. Residents who would have qualified for the discounts in opting-in states never got them.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; all 7 cosponsors were House Democrats and there is no record of Republican support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill would force manufacturers to pay Medicaid-style rebates on drugs sold through state discount programs, or exit the entire Medicaid rebate agreement. Their interest in blocking it ran against residents who would have paid lower prices.
States would get a voluntary new tool to lower drug costs for residents using rebate money, with no mandate to spend state funds.
Discount programs route more price-sensitive purchases through pharmacies, which would fill them at reduced reimbursement; volume and margin would move in opposite directions.
